name: Hook Strip to Re-Guard
description: Master Hook Strip to Re-Guard escape from Crab Ride Bottom. Step-by-step technique to strip hooks and recover guard. Success rates: Beginner 30%, Intermediate 50%, Advanced 65%.
overview:
The Hook Strip to Re-Guard is a fundamental defensive technique executed from Crab Ride Bottom, designed to strip the opponent's controlling hook and immediately recover to a guard position. This technique is essential for anyone facing crab ride attacks, as it addresses the primary control mechanism that prevents guard recovery. The movement combines precise hand placement on the opponent's ankle or instep with explosive hip movement to create separation and establish defensive frames.

Strategically, this escape represents the first line of defense against back attacks from crab ride. When your opponent has established one hook while working toward full back control, stripping that hook before the second hook lands dramatically changes the positional dynamic. The technique requires understanding that you are not simply removing a leg - you are creating a chain reaction where hook removal leads immediately to hip escape and guard establishment. Hesitation after stripping the hook results in immediate re-attachment.

The timing of this technique is crucial. The optimal window occurs when your opponent shifts their weight forward to establish grips or attempt the second hook. During this moment, their hook becomes lighter and more susceptible to being stripped. Advanced practitioners learn to bait these moments by creating false openings that draw the top player's attention forward, then explosively executing the strip and guard recovery in one fluid sequence.
key_principles: Strip the hook using the same-side hand cupping the ankle from inside, pushing toward the mat and away from your hip
Combine hook stripping with immediate hip escape movement - never strip statically
Protect your neck with the opposite hand throughout the stripping motion to prevent choke setups
Direct your hips away from the hooked side as you strip to create maximum separation distance
Immediately insert a butterfly hook or establish half guard frames before opponent can re-establish control
Use explosive movement timing rather than sustained wrestling - speed defeats grip re-establishment
Maintain chest-to-mat connection during the strip to prevent being elevated and rolled
setup_requirements: Opponent has established crab ride with one hook inserted on your hip or thigh
You maintain turtle base with at least one hand free to address the hook
Your neck is protected or you have momentary safety from choke threats
Opponent's weight is distributed forward or they are reaching for secondary control
You have identified the exact position of their hook foot relative to your body

execution_steps.description: Before addressing the hook, use your far-side hand to control opponent's choking arm or establish a frame against their bicep. Your chin must be tucked tightly against your chest to prevent rear naked choke setups during the escape.
execution_steps.timing: Immediately upon recognizing crab ride establishment

execution_steps.description: Identify the exact position of opponent's hook foot. Feel whether it is wrapped around your thigh, hooked at your hip crease, or floating near your knee. This determines your grip placement for the strip.

Using your same-side hand (the hand on the hooked side), reach down and cup opponent's ankle or heel from the inside. Your fingers wrap around the Achilles tendon area while your palm contacts the back of their ankle.

In one explosive motion, push their hook toward the mat and away from your hip while simultaneously executing a powerful hip escape in the opposite direction. Your hips shoot away from the hook as their leg is stripped.

As separation is created, immediately insert your near-side leg as a butterfly hook or establish knee shield position. This leg must enter the space before opponent can advance or re-attach their hook.

Complete the transition by facing your opponent and establishing proper guard frames. Your hands create distance while your hips continue moving to fully establish half guard or butterfly guard position with proper defensive structure.

common_counters.counter: Opponent drives forward and establishes chest pressure before you can strip
common_counters.your_response: Abandon the strip attempt and focus on preventing the second hook. Use Granby roll or forward roll escape instead if flattened

common_counters.counter: Opponent immediately re-inserts hook as you strip by following your hip movement
common_counters.your_response: Continue hip escape motion and use your inserted butterfly hook to create elevation, sweeping or off-balancing before they settle

common_counters.counter: Opponent transitions to body triangle or back control during your strip attempt
common_counters.your_response: If you feel second hook entering during strip, immediately address the back control with hand fighting rather than completing guard recovery

common_counters.counter: Opponent attacks neck with arm-in guillotine as you turn toward them
common_counters.your_response: Keep chin tucked throughout turn and use far hand to frame against their bicep preventing guillotine depth

common_errors.error: Attempting to strip the hook before securing neck protection
common_errors.consequence: Opponent capitalizes on your divided attention to lock in rear naked choke or bow and arrow grip
common_errors.correction: Always establish neck safety with your far hand before reaching for the hook with your near hand

common_errors.error: Stripping the hook without simultaneous hip escape movement
common_errors.consequence: Hook is removed but opponent immediately re-inserts because no distance was created
common_errors.correction: Treat the strip and hip escape as one inseparable motion - never strip statically

common_errors.error: Failing to immediately insert defensive hook after stripping
common_errors.consequence: Opponent advances to a worse position (mount, back control) through the created space
common_errors.correction: Your leg must enter the space the moment their hook exits - there is no pause between strip and guard insertion

common_errors.error: Using wrong hand to strip (far hand instead of same-side hand)
common_errors.consequence: Creates shoulder exposure that allows opponent to flatten you or take your back
common_errors.correction: Always strip with the same-side hand while the far hand maintains frames or neck protection

common_errors.error: Reaching behind your back to find the hook rather than feeling for it
common_errors.consequence: Telegraphs the strip attempt and allows opponent to secure deeper hooks or advance position
common_errors.correction: Develop tactile awareness to locate hooks by feel, keeping movement minimal and explosive

training_progressions.description: Practice the hook strip mechanics in isolation. Partner establishes loose crab ride, you locate and strip the hook using proper hand placement. Focus on the cupping grip and push direction. No hip escape yet - just the stripping motion.

Combine strip with hip escape as one motion. Partner holds position with light resistance. Practice the timing trigger - stripping when you feel their weight shift forward. Add the butterfly hook insertion after the strip.

Chain the hook strip with guard recovery variations. If half guard, practice knee shield establishment. If butterfly, practice immediate elevation. Partner provides moderate resistance and attempts to re-insert hooks.

Positional sparring from crab ride bottom. Full resistance with partner actively working to complete back take. Practice recognizing windows, executing under pressure, and recovering to functional guard positions.

variants_and_adaptations.description: When opponent's hook is particularly deep or strong, briefly release neck protection to use both hands on the ankle. Execute extremely fast to minimize neck exposure. Both hands grip the ankle and strip toward the mat while hips explode away.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When single-hand strip repeatedly fails against strong hook or larger opponent

variants_and_adaptations.description: Instead of stripping then escaping, use the strip attempt to initiate a Granby roll. As you cup the ankle, roll over your shoulder toward the hooked side while stripping. You end facing opponent in guard rather than escaping laterally.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When opponent has heavy chest pressure making lateral hip escape difficult

variants_and_adaptations.description: Strip the hook while executing a wrestling sit-through. As the hook clears, your hips rotate through to face opponent. Often leads directly to single leg or butterfly guard rather than half guard.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When you have underhook control on the opposite side enabling the sit-through rotation

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the primary goal of Hook Strip to Re-Guard?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The primary goal is to remove the opponent's controlling hook from crab ride position and immediately establish a guard position (typically half guard or butterfly guard) before they can re-establish control or advance to full back control. This converts a defensive scramble into an established guard where you have structured defense.

knowledge_assessment.question: What position do you start Hook Strip to Re-Guard from?
knowledge_assessment.answer: This technique starts from Crab Ride Bottom, where you are in turtle position and your opponent has established one hook on your hip or thigh while controlling your upper body from the side. They are working to establish the second hook for full back control.

knowledge_assessment.question: What are the key grips needed for Hook Strip to Re-Guard?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The primary grip is a cupping grip on opponent's ankle using your same-side hand (the hand on the hooked side). Your fingers wrap around the Achilles tendon area while your palm contacts the back of their ankle. Your far hand should be controlling opponent's choking arm or framing against their bicep for neck protection.

knowledge_assessment.question: How do you counter an opponent attempting Hook Strip to Re-Guard?
knowledge_assessment.answer: As the top player, counter by driving your chest pressure forward and down the moment you feel them reaching for your hook. Simultaneously work to insert your second hook. If they successfully strip, immediately follow their hip movement and reattach before they can establish guard frames. Body triangle threat can also prevent strip attempts.

knowledge_assessment.question: When is the best time to attempt Hook Strip to Re-Guard?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The optimal timing is when opponent shifts their weight forward to establish grips, reach for the second hook, or adjust their upper body control. During these moments their hook becomes lighter and more susceptible to being stripped. You can bait these moments by creating false openings that draw their attention and weight forward.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent immediately re-inserts their hook after you strip it - what adjustment do you make?
knowledge_assessment.answer: If opponent follows your hip movement and re-inserts, you did not create enough distance with your hip escape or were too slow inserting your defensive hook. The adjustment is to make the strip and hip escape more explosive and simultaneous, and ensure your butterfly hook or knee shield enters the space immediately as their hook exits. There should be no gap in timing.

knowledge_assessment.question: Why must you secure neck protection before attempting the hook strip?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The hook strip requires you to reach down toward your hips with one hand, which creates opportunity for opponent to attack your neck if your far hand is not controlling their choking arm. Attempting to strip without neck protection invites rear naked choke setups or allows opponent to collapse your posture. The far hand must maintain defensive frames throughout the stripping motion.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the most critical directional element of the hook strip movement?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The hook must be pushed toward the mat and away from your hip - not simply pulled off. The downward-and-away direction breaks the hooking angle while your hips explode in the opposite direction. Pulling the hook toward you or upward fails because it does not break the hooking mechanic and keeps the leg in position to immediately re-attach.

knowledge_assessment.question: How does the hook strip integrate with the broader turtle escape system?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Hook Strip to Re-Guard is the primary response when opponent has one hook but has not completed the back take. It exists alongside Granby rolls, forward rolls, and standing escapes as turtle defense options. The hook strip specifically addresses the hooking leg while Granby addresses heavy chest pressure. Recognizing which escape fits the current threat is key to systematic turtle defense.

knowledge_assessment.question: If your strip attempt fails and opponent drives forward heavily, what should your contingency response be?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Abandon the strip and immediately transition to Granby roll or forward roll escape. When opponent commits heavy chest pressure, the lateral hip escape becomes nearly impossible. The Granby uses their forward pressure against them by rolling over your shoulder. Do not continue fighting a losing battle with the strip - recognize the changing situation and select the appropriate alternative escape.

safety_considerations: The Hook Strip to Re-Guard is a relatively safe technique with low injury risk when practiced correctly. The primary safety concern is neck vulnerability during the stripping motion - always ensure neck protection before reaching for the hook. During drilling, partners should avoid explosive re-hooks that could catch training partners off guard. When practicing at higher intensity, be aware that rapid direction changes can strain the lower back if executed without proper core engagement. Tap immediately if opponent secures a choke during your escape attempt rather than trying to complete the technique while being strangled.
position_integration: Hook Strip to Re-Guard is a critical component of the turtle survival and escape system, specifically addressing crab ride attacks before they develop into full back control. This technique connects the defensive turtle position to the offensive guard position, representing the first decision point in the turtle defense flowchart. When successful, it leads to half guard or butterfly guard where you can begin attacking. When it fails, you must recognize the changing situation and flow to secondary escapes like Granby roll or forward roll. Mastery of this technique reduces the effectiveness of modern wrestling-based back attacks that rely on crab ride as a transitional control point.
